lesson.title: The Secret Race to Split the Atom
lesson.summary: The Manhattan Project was the vast, secret American program that developed the atomic bomb during World War II, driven initially by fear that Nazi Germany might build one first.
lesson.body:
Even before the United States formally entered World War II, a small number of scientists warned American leaders about a terrifying possibility. In 1939, physicist Albert Einstein signed a letter, largely drafted by physicist Leo Szilard, urging President Roosevelt to fund research into nuclear chain reactions, warning that Nazi Germany, which had scientists capable of similar work, might be pursuing an extraordinarily powerful new weapon based on splitting uranium atoms. That warning helped set in motion a research effort that, after the U.S. entry into the war, grew into one of the largest and most secretive projects the government had ever undertaken.

The effort became known as the Manhattan Project, named for the Army Corps of Engineers district that initially oversaw it. General Leslie Groves directed the project's massive logistics and construction, while physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer led the scientific team assembled at a secret laboratory built at Los Alamos, New Mexico, to design and build the actual weapon. The project ultimately spanned multiple secret sites across the country, including a huge uranium enrichment facility at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, and a plutonium production complex at Hanford, Washington. It employed well over one hundred thousand people at its peak, the vast majority of whom had no idea what the project's final purpose actually was, working in strict compartmentalized secrecy and costing roughly two billion dollars, an enormous sum at the time.

On July 16, 1945, scientists detonated the world's first nuclear weapon in a test codenamed Trinity, in the desert near Alamogordo, New Mexico. The explosion, far more powerful than anyone present had fully anticipated, confirmed that the weapon worked and that humanity now possessed a wholly new category of destructive power.

The Trinity test came only months after Germany had already surrendered, meaning the original fear that drove the project, that Germany might build the bomb first, was no longer the concern it had once been. By the time the bomb was ready, the war that remained was against Japan, and American leaders now faced a decision about whether and how to use this new weapon to try to end that war.
